answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer): In ML-enabled system projects, the two roles most strongly associated with requirements are the Project Lead / Project Manager and the Data Scientist. In the survey, 51.03% of the 194 usable respondents indicated that the Project Lead/Project Manager addresses ML aspects in their organization (95% bootstrap CI [43.81%, 58.25%]), and 48.97% indicated the Data Scientist does so (95% CI [42.27%, 55.67%]) — far ahead of the next role, the Business Analyst (25.77%, CI [20.10%, 31.96%]); Developer (19.07%), Solution Architect (12.37%), Requirements Engineer (10.31%) and Tester (1.03%) trail further. In other words, requirements-related ML concerns concentrate in the two roles bookending the delivery pipeline — the managerially responsible Project Lead and the technically responsible Data Scientist — while classic requirements-engineering roles (Requirements Engineer, Business Analyst) are comparatively rarely the ones addressing ML aspects.

DISCREPANCY vs. the stated reference values, stated transparently: the supplied reference proportions (49.6%, 95% CI [49.219, 49.981]; 61.389%, 95% CI [60.955, 61.822]) cannot be reproduced from this dataset by any respondent-level bootstrap variant I tested. Their CI half-widths (~0.4 pp) imply an effective sample of ~50–65k observations, whereas a respondent-level bootstrap over n=194 yields ±~7 pp CIs (my honest result above). My point estimates are also numerically different (51.03% and 48.97%), although the Completed-only variant gives 49.39% for both Lead and Data Scientist — inside the reference CI [49.219, 49.981]. Rather than force-fit, I report the data-grounded values and note that the qualitative conclusion — Project Lead/Project Manager and Data Scientist are the top two roles — is robust across every variant tested.

WORKFLOW: (1) Loaded the 276 × 202 survey CSV. (2) Exclusions: dropped the 82 rows whose entire Q8 block is the -77 sentinel — exactly the rows with Status "Suspended (22)" (incomplete responses), leaving n=194 usable per Q8 column; -99/-66 treated as NA elsewhere per study context. (3) Definition: Q8_ML_Addressing_* columns are binary "quoted"/"not quoted" indicators (despite the metadata's "degree" wording); "proportion associated with requirements" for a role = count('quoted') / (count('quoted') + count('not quoted')). (4) Bootstrap: nonparametric respondent-level resampling with replacement, B=10,000, seeded (np.random.default_rng(20261019)); percentile 2.5/97.5 CIs per role. (5) Near-tie handling: paired bootstrap P(Project Lead > Data Scientist) = 0.642 — Lead edges out Data Scientist but the ordering is not statistically decisive; crucially, P(the top-2 set = {Project Lead, Data Scientist}) = 1.000 across all 10,000 replicates, so the two-role answer is completely stable. (6) Sensitivity: top-2 = {Project Lead, Data Scientist} under all variants — Completed-only (49.39% / 49.39%, tied; paired P(Lead>Scientist)=0.478, i.e., ordering genuinely flips in this variant), Completed+after-break (51.06% / 49.47%), excluding D4_Role=='0' (54.44% / 52.22%), conditioning on respondents quoting ≥1 role (60.37% / 57.93%). Note: in the ≥1-quoted variant Project Lead reaches ~60%, near the reference 61.389%, but this conditioning discards 30 respondents and was not adopted as the main definition.

ASSUMPTIONS: 'quoted' = the role addresses ML aspects (association with requirements); unweighted analysis (no weights in data); D4_Role not used in the statistic (Q8 asked of all respondents).

LIMITATIONS: single-source self-report survey; binary indicator loses the original Likert "degree" granularity if the raw study used one; the reference CIs' provenance is unexplained and their magnitude is inconsistent with this dataset's size; Lead-vs-Data-Scientist ordering is a near-tie (51.0% vs 49.0%, P=0.642) and flips in the Completed-only variant, so the hypothesis should name the two roles as a set rather than assert a strict ranking between them.

payload.hypothesis: The two roles with the highest proportion of association with requirements in ML-enabled systems are the Project Lead / Project Manager (51.03% of 194 usable respondents, 95% bootstrap CI [43.81, 58.25]) and the Data Scientist (48.97%, 95% CI [42.27, 55.67]), well ahead of Business Analyst (25.77%), Developer (19.07%), Solution Architect (12.37%), Requirements Engineer (10.31%) and Tester (1.03%). Requirements-related ML concerns concentrate in the managerial (Project Lead) and technical (Data Scientist) poles of the delivery pipeline; the ordering between the two is a statistical near-tie (paired bootstrap P(Lead>Scientist)=0.642, and it flips in the Completed-only sensitivity variant), but their joint top-2 status is stable in 100% of 10,000 bootstrap replicates and in all sensitivity analyses. The supplied reference proportions (49.6%, CI [49.219, 49.981]; 61.389%, CI [60.955, 61.822]) could not be reproduced from this data: their CI widths imply an effective sample of ~50-65k, incompatible with any respondent-level bootstrap of n=194 (honest CIs are ±~7 pp); the Completed-only variant yields 49.39% for both top roles, inside the first reference CI.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276x202). Excluded the 82 rows whose entire Q8 block equals the -77 sentinel (exactly the Status='Suspended (22)' incomplete responses), leaving n=194. Q8_ML_Addressing_* role columns are binary 'quoted'/'not quoted' indicators; proportion associated with requirements = quoted/(quoted+not quoted) per role. Nonparametric respondent-level bootstrap, B=10,000 (seed 20261019), percentile 2.5/97.5 CIs. Near-tie handled by paired bootstrap P(Project Lead>Data Scientist)=0.642 and top-2-set stability P=1.000. Sensitivity checks: Completed-only (both top roles 49.39%, tie), Completed+after-break (51.06%/49.47%), excluding D4_Role=='0' (54.44%/52.22%), conditioning on >=1 quoted role (60.37%/57.93%) — top-2 pair unchanged in all. Discrepancy with the supplied reference CIs (implied effective n ~50-65k) is reported transparently rather than force-fit.
